claims.text: A dense network of interfaces in HEA multilayer coatings impedes dislocation motion.
A dense network of interfaces in HEA multilayer coatings slows diffusion-driven processes.
Interface-induced impediments increase the effective activation barrier for creep and stress relaxation.
Impeded dislocation motion and slower diffusion reduce time-dependent plastic deformation at elevated temperature.
Layer thickness and interface density can be varied systematically in otherwise compositionally equivalent HEA multilayer coatings.
Nanoindentation and micropillar compression can characterize time-dependent deformation at small scales.
The relevant protective-coating service range is approximately 600–900 °C.
Stress and temperature govern creep-related atomic rearrangement, with increasing temperature and stress accelerating creep.
Interfaces between distinct HEA layers are strong barriers to both dislocation glide and climb.
Interfaces act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Pinned dislocations are forced to bow or accumulate at interfaces.
Interfaces slow dislocation climb.
Slower dislocation motion limits time-dependent plastic flow and increases creep resistance.
Thinner individual layers correspond to higher interface density.
Higher-interface-density HEA multilayers will show less indentation creep depth or micropillar creep strain than monolithic or coarser-layer references.
Significant interdiffusion and interface coarsening can occur after sufficiently high-temperature or prolonged exposure.
Interdiffusion and interface coarsening diminish the creep-resistance benefit attributed to interfaces.
Interfacial lattice misfit may influence or dominate creep resistance.
Chemical gradients and other interfacial microstructural features may dominate creep resistance.
Failure to observe an association between interface density, suppressed time-dependent deformation, and slowed dislocation activity would invalidate the proposed interface-driven mechanism.
